extracted.intended_audience: general readers (media consumers), journalists, educators, and policymakers interested in media manipulation and misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for recognizing, understanding, and responding to fake-news websites (methods they use, signals of fakery, motivations, and platform/government/educational responses), with emphasis on U.S. examples and election cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: deliberate publication of hoaxes/propaganda/disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news websites deliberately publish hoaxes, propaganda, and disinformation to drive web traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sites are distinguished from news satire as fake news articles are usually fabricated to deliberately mislead readers, either for profit or more ambiguous reasons, such as disinformation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fake news from satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is usually fabricated to deliberately mislead; news satire may be humorous but is expected to signal itself as satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire sites have received criticism for not properly notifying readers that they are publishing false or satirical content, since many readers have been duped by seemingly legitimate articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait headlines / sensational titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Article titles that are incredible or exaggerated, prompting the user to click and read more; often withhold significant information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook defines clickbait 'as headlines that withhold significant amounts of information and mislead the user'. Clickbait often leads to exaggerated or fake titles and is commonly used to trick users who cannot tell if the article is real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of out-of-context or manipulated images
rubrics_metrics.description: Images chosen or edited to inflame readers or to create a false sense of legitimacy for an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Out-of-context or manipulated images can cause readers to incorrectly assume an article's legitimacy, often due to their inflammatory image choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation of legitimate news organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying website formatting, names, authorship, or creating near-exact copies of established news sites to appear legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impersonation can be crude (spoofing names like ABCnews.com.co) or exact copies that trick viewers into believing the website is an official organization (examples: Bloomberg.ma, cnn-trending.com). Exact copies can fool users who don't examine details closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typosquatting / domain spoofing
rubrics_metrics.description: Registering domains that exploit common misspellings or use deceptive top-level domains (e.g., .com.co) to catch accidental traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typosquatters monitor clicks to 'typo' domain names and then monetize high accidental traffic with advertising. Fake news sites often exploit misspellings or slight misphrasings and abuse of top-level domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity / lack of transparent authorship or 'About Us'
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that pretend to have reporters or omit an 'About Us' page; authorship and ownership are opaque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since authors are not actual reporters, many fake news sites either invent reporter identities or simply do not include transparency pages. When publicized by legitimate organizations they may receive perceived legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic motivation: ad revenue-driven fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating fabricated stories primarily to attract clicks and ad revenue rather than inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: writers earning significant monthly ad revenue (e.g., Paul Horner said he made $10,000 per month). Clickbait and virality are monetized; articles may appear legitimate at the top and become absurd further down to retain ad clicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological motivation: influence and campaign support
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing false content to advance political or ideological goals rather than profit alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some producers create pro-candidate or issue-driven false stories to support campaigns (examples cited from 2016 election cycle). Motivations can be mixed (profit + ideology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style: legitimate-looking lead, increasing absurdity deeper in article
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles structured to appear credible at the beginning but become increasingly absurd, to fool cursory readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A noted tactic: make the top of an article seem legitimate while inserting absurd or fabricated details later so that a casual reader will accept the story without reading fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated quotes/transcripts and invented facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Making up quotes, transcripts, or factual claims (e.g., fake leaked speeches or endorsements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include fake transcripts purporting to be from politicians; fact-checkers have debunked many such fabrications. Fabricated supporting 'evidence' is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated site networks and hidden ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sites owned/operated by the same person or company to amplify messages and mask origin (use of pseudonyms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may use pseudonyms and company structures (e.g., Disinfomedia, Jestin Coler) to run many fake sites and to seed content across domains, making detection and attribution harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-site referencing / mutual citation to feign legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake sites reference or link to one another to create the appearance of corroboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some networks and individual sites frequently referenced each other, boosting apparent credibility (National Report and News Examiner referenced each other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploiting search engines and SEO to appear authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: Using search-optimization tactics so false stories rank highly for relevant queries, thereby reaching users searching for authoritative info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 70News temporarily ranked highly for 'final election vote count' and fooled searchers. Search algorithms use hundreds of factors; manipulators exploit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-media amplification and algorithmic virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Using social platforms' sharing dynamics and algorithms to achieve massive distribution—sometimes outperforming real news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies found top fake stories on Facebook received more engagement than top real news stories in late 2016. Viral tweets and cross-platform promotion can rapidly amplify falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fake/inauthentic accounts and AI-generated media
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploying inauthentic pages, accounts, and AI-generated images to appear real and avoid detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fake networks have used accounts that managed to avoid detection and used photos generated with the aid of artificial intelligence (noted in the 2020 cycle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators for consumers: verification badges and visual cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize platform verification (blue checkmarks), author transparency, source lists, and consistent contact/about information as signals of legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research showed many students didn't recognize verification badges; fact-checking organizations publish guides on how to spot fake news. Lack of verification, missing about/contact info, or strange domain choices are warning signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party fact-checking and platform labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms can flag disputed stories and surface third-party fact-checkers to assess veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook implemented a system where flagged stories are sent to third-party organizations (e.g., ABC News, AP, FactCheck.org, PolitiFact, Snopes) to check veracity; failed checks result in lower news feed priority and captions like 'disputed by 3rd party fact-checkers'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform mitigation strategies: reduce financial incentives and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms can change ad policies, demote disputed content, and hire content reviewers to reduce incentives and spread of fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facebook and Google used ad policy and ranking changes to limit fake-news monetization; Facebook hired thousands of moderators and admitted shortcomings in preventing meddling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational interventions and media literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching students and the public skills to distinguish real from fake news via classroom exercises and curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: classroom 'fake news challenge', OECD 'global competencies' testing, partnerships (Newsela/American Press Institute). Education aims to give long-term discernment skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental and legislative responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative and government efforts to investigate, fund counter-disinformation, and create inter-agency responses to foreign propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. legislative actions cited include travel/investigations by Senate committees, funding authorized in the National Defense Authorization Act, and proposals like the Countering Foreign Propaganda and Disinformation Act; government units have been proposed, created, or canceled (e.g., the State Dept Counter-Disinformation Team).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on and limits of fact-checking organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers compile lists of fake sites and issue identification guides, but their coverage and influence have practical limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the election many fact-checking websites teamed with platforms to check articles; they also publish lists and guides to help consumers identify fake sites. The article notes fact-checkers' lists and resources.
